label: Natural Gradient and Singular Learning
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 279 through 314 and asks how learning changes when parameter space is a Riemannian statistical manifold rather than a Euclidean box. Natural gradient is steepest descent in the Fisher metric, and the same metric exposes the singular regions where ordinary learning stalls.

label: Steepest Descent Needs a Metric
notes: Steepest descent is only well defined after we fix what a unit step means. In Euclidean coordinates the fair ball is a sphere and the steepest direction is minus the gradient. On a statistical manifold the fair ball is the Fisher ellipse, so the honest steepest direction is reweighted by the inverse metric.

label: The Natural Gradient
notes: Solving the constrained steepest-descent problem in the Fisher metric gives the natural gradient: the ordinary gradient multiplied by the inverse Fisher matrix. It is the direction that decreases loss fastest per unit of movement in distribution space, making it invariant to smooth reparameterization of the model.

label: Euclidean vs Natural Paths
notes: On a quadratic loss with anisotropic curvature, ordinary descent zig-zags across narrow valleys and must take tiny steps for stability. Natural gradient rescales by the metric, turning the elongated bowl into an isotropic one, so the path heads almost straight to the optimum in far fewer iterations.

label: Why Natural Gradient Wins
notes: The metric view explains the advantage: natural gradient is a coordinate-free contraction in distribution space. The Fisher matrix corrects for how stretched each direction is statistically, so anisotropy that traps ordinary descent is absorbed. The same rescaling restores informative directions when activations saturate and Euclidean gradients vanish.

label: Hessian Geometry and the Saddle Trap
notes: Newton geometry uses the Hessian, which can be indefinite away from a minimum. At a saddle the signed Hessian points the negative-curvature coordinate toward the saddle, stalling escape. Replacing each Hessian eigenvalue by its absolute value keeps curvature scaling while flipping the unstable direction into an escape direction.

label: Mirror Descent as Dual Natural Gradient
notes: Mirror descent with negative entropy on the simplex is natural gradient in disguise. The mirror map sends probabilities to log coordinates, where each step is an ordinary gradient update plus a renormalizing constant. The primal simplex path stays positive and normalized while the dual increments are straight, with metric equal to the Hessian of the potential.

label: Singular Models and Non-Identifiability
notes: A singular model has parameters that produce identical distributions, so the Fisher matrix degenerates and loses rank. The one-hidden-unit map v tanh(w x) shows this: when v is zero, w is invisible, and when w is zero, v is invisible. These unidentifiable axes are exactly where regular asymptotic theory breaks down.

label: The Geometry of the Singular Set
notes: The unidentifiable directions form a singular set, a cross of axes in the parameter plane where Fisher eigenvalues collapse to zero. Along these axes the metric ellipse degenerates into a flat sliver. The heatmap of the smallest eigenvalue shows the cross directly, marking where the inverse metric blows up.

label: Plateaus and Blow-Down Coordinates
notes: Near the singular set ordinary gradients shrink in the identifiable direction, producing long plateaus where loss barely moves yet many iterations pass. Blow-down coordinates treat the collapsed set as a single behavior point, restoring ordinary dynamics. The metric tells us which directions are redundant rather than genuinely flat.

label: Learning Coefficient and RLCT
notes: Singular learning theory replaces the parameter count by the real log canonical threshold, the learning coefficient lambda. The Bayes free energy grows like lambda times log n, and for singular models lambda is smaller than half the dimension, so singular models can generalize better than their parameter count suggests.

label: Damping and Takeaways
notes: Practical natural gradient solves a damped system with the inverse of the Fisher matrix plus lambda times the identity, trading a tiny bias for stability near collapsed eigenvalues. The chapter lesson: choose the metric deliberately, watch rank and eigenvalues, and move in behavior space rather than wandering through redundant parameters.
